summary:
Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity under Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, which carries a maximum of five years' imprisonment. The provision is enforced: in September 2018 four LGBT people, two women and two men, were detained in Dakar on charges of "acts against the order of nature" after videos of them circulated, part of a wave of politically motivated detentions in the run-up to the 2019 elections.

A campaign to raise the maximum penalty to 15 years has run since 2020, with anti-LGBT forces pressing for the increase as of July 2024. The maximum sentence remains five years; the proposal has not been reported as enacted.

Official hostility extends to speech on the subject. A political activist and a preacher were jailed and fined 100,000 CFA francs each after posting a video attacking opposition leader Ousmane Sonko for allowing a visiting French politician to express support for same-sex marriage. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report on Senegal listed pre-electoral violence, torture, and violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the country's major human-rights problems.

Violence by non-state actors is documented at extreme scale. In November 2023 the body of a 31-year-old man, named locally as Cheikh Fall, was dug up from a cemetery and burned in the street after it became known that he was gay. Four men were arrested in connection with the incident; images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathered around the fire.
tangentialFactors:
Enforcement in Senegal has a demonstrably political rhythm. The September 2018 detentions in Dakar came amid a wave of arrests ahead of the 2019 elections, and the US State Department's 2012 report identified pre-electoral violence as one of the country's major human-rights problems alongside anti-LGBT abuse. Travellers should expect the intensity of policing around LGBT people to rise during election periods rather than remain constant.

The Sonko affair shows that the sensitivity runs to association as well as conduct: the two men jailed were punished for criticising a politician for giving a platform to a foreign figure who voiced support for same-sex marriage, not for any sexual conduct of their own. Public discussion that appears to tolerate same-sex relations can itself draw criminal penalties.

The pending debate over raising the sentence from five to fifteen years keeps the legal environment unsettled. Abuses against LGBT people are described as commonplace in the country, and the November 2023 exhumation drew a crowd of hundreds, indicating that mob action can occur with broad public participation while arrests follow after the fact.
localsOnly:
Senegalese residents live under the same Article 319 provision, and enforcement has reached women as well as men: two of the four people detained in Dakar in September 2018 were women.

Residents face penalties for speech as well as conduct. The activist and the preacher jailed over the video attacking Ousmane Sonko were fined 100,000 CFA francs (about $165, £130) each in addition to imprisonment.

Four men were arrested in connection with the November 2023 burning of Cheikh Fall's exhumed body, though the gathering around the fire numbered in the hundreds. Anti-LGBT forces have campaigned since 2020 to raise the prison term for gay sex to fifteen years, and were still pushing for it as of July 2024.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced information on legal gender recognition or the change of sex markers on Senegalese identity documents, on hate-crime provisions covering gender identity, on recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriages, on entry or visa screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status, on access to gender-affirming medical care, or on facilities and restroom rules. These are unresolved rather than absent from Senegalese law.

Whether Article 319 has been applied specifically to transgender people, as distinct from cisgender men and women, is not sourced here; the 2018 detentions involved two women and two men but the reporting does not identify any of them as trans.

The legislative status of the proposed fifteen-year penalty is unresolved beyond July 2024, the date of the most recent source in the inventory. The US State Department human rights material dates from 2012 and does not establish current conditions on its own.
